In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[graph theory]], a '''path graph''' (or '''linear graph''') is a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] whose [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] can be listed in the order {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub>, ''v''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''v<sub>n</sub>''}} such that the [[edge (graph theory)|edge]]s are {{math|{''v<sub>i</sub>'', ''v''<sub>''i''+1</sub>}}} where {{math|1=''i'' = 1, 2, ..., ''n'' − 1}}.  Equivalently, a path with at least two vertices is [[connectivity (graph theory)|connected]] and has two terminal vertices (vertices of [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] 1), while all others (if any) have degree 2.

Paths are often important in their role as [[Glossary of graph theory#Subgraphs|subgraphs]] of other graphs, in which case they are called [[path (graph theory)|path]]s in that graph.  A path is a particularly simple example of a [[tree (graph theory)|tree]], and in fact the paths are exactly the trees in which no vertex has degree 3 or more. A [[disjoint union of graphs|disjoint union]] of paths is called a [[linear forest]].

Paths are fundamental concepts of graph theory, described in the introductory sections of most graph theory texts. See, for example, Bondy and Murty (1976), Gibbons (1985), or Diestel (2005).

== As Dynkin diagrams ==

In [[algebra]], path graphs appear as the [[Dynkin diagram]]s of type A.  As such, they classify the [[root system]] of type A and the [[Weyl group]] of type A, which is the [[symmetric group]].
